lesson.title: Joining Molecules, Releasing Water: How Condensation Builds Polymers
lesson.summary: A condensation reaction links two monomers together by forming a new covalent bond between their functional groups and releasing a water molecule, and it is the basic chemical step behind building every carbohydrate, protein, and nucleic acid polymer.
lesson.body:
A condensation reaction, also called a dehydration synthesis reaction, is the chemical step cells use to link two monomers together into a growing polymer chain. The name describes exactly what happens: as a new covalent bond forms between two monomers, a molecule of water is released as a byproduct, condensing out of the reaction. This single reaction type, repeated over and over, is how carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids are actually assembled from their monomers.

The mechanism draws directly on the functional groups covered earlier. Typically, one monomer contributes a hydroxyl group and the other contributes a hydrogen atom from one of its own functional groups. During the reaction, the hydroxyl from one monomer combines with the hydrogen from the other, and together they leave as a water molecule. Removing that hydroxyl and hydrogen frees up a bonding position on each of the two monomers, and a new covalent bond forms directly between them where the water used to be. The two monomers, once separate, are now permanently linked.

Protein assembly is a clear example. Recall that every amino acid carries both a carboxyl group and an amino group. When two amino acids join, the carboxyl group of the first amino acid reacts with the amino group of the second: a hydroxyl from the carboxyl group and a hydrogen from the amino group combine into a released water molecule, and a new covalent bond, called a peptide bond, forms directly between the carbon of the first amino acid's carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the second amino acid's amino group. Repeating this reaction hundreds of times, always adding one more amino acid and releasing one more water molecule, builds a polypeptide chain.

Carbohydrate assembly follows the identical logic with a different pair of functional groups. Two glucose monomers, each bearing several hydroxyl groups, can react so that a hydroxyl group from one glucose molecule combines with a hydrogen from a hydroxyl group on the neighboring glucose molecule, releasing water and forming a new covalent bond called a glycosidic linkage directly between the two sugar rings. This is exactly how the disaccharide maltose forms from two glucose units, and how repeating this same reaction thousands of times builds the long glucose polymers glycogen and cellulose described earlier, with the specific geometry of the linkage determining which polymer results.

In a real cell, condensation reactions rarely happen spontaneously at a useful rate; joining monomers together is energetically uphill, so these reactions are catalyzed by specific enzymes, and in many cases the process is coupled to energy released from ATP to make it favorable. This enzymatic control is also what allows a cell to build very specific polymers, a particular protein sequence or a particular polysaccharide, rather than random combinations. Every condensation reaction, though, is reversible in principle, and reversing it, breaking a polymer back down into its monomers by adding water back in, is the hydrolysis reaction covered next.
